healthInfo.qualityNotes: Excellent healthcare system with high-quality hospitals, especially in major cities (Rome, Milan, Florence). English is spoken at larger hospitals but less so in smaller clinics. Public healthcare is free or low-cost for residents; tourists can access emergency care at public hospitals.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-8pm. Some close for lunch (1-4pm). In large cities, some pharmacies are open 24/7. Look for the green cross sign (Croce Verde). Farmacia turns into a farmaceutico di turno (on-duty pharmacy) after hours for urgent needs.
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Pharmacies are widely available. Many medications require a prescription. The pharmacist (farmacista) can advise on minor ailments. Some OTC products like ibuprofen and paracetamol are available without prescription.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by an Italian doctor. Italy has stricter rules than some EU countries — many antibiotics and prescription medications require an Italian prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Italy. Some codeine products are restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring an Italian prescription or special import authorization from the Ministry of Health.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines (Valium/diazepam, Xanax/alprazolam)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A valid prescription is required. Italy closely monitors these medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Italy but heavily restricted to specific conditions and only available through hospital pharmacies.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English/Italian listing all medications with generic names. Bring sufficient supply for your trip in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry the prescription documentation at all times. EU citizens should carry the EHIC card.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: Italy's public hospitals provide emergency care free of charge to all people. For non-emergency care, you'll need travel insurance. Carry your insurance details and a 24/7 emergency contact number. Pharmacies may direct you to a hospital for serious conditions.

recommended: Hepatitis A (for extended stays or close contact with locals)
Meningococcal disease (for students or long-term stays)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Italy. In some southern regions, tap water may have a strong chlorine taste but is safe. Bottled water (acqua minerale) is widely available.
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: Italy has excellent food safety. Be cautious with raw eggs (mayonnaise, tiramisu) in rural areas. Wild mushrooms (funghi) are popular — only eat those verified by a licensed mycologist. Be cautious with buffalo mozzarella from non-reputable sources. Food in restaurants and tourist areas is very safe.
sources: Italy Ministry of Health (Ministero della Salute)
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: Italy is known for elective procedures, fertility treatments, and cosmetic surgery tourism, particularly in Milan and Rome.

healthcare.costForTourists: EU citizens get emergency care with EHIC card. Non-EU tourists pay — ER visit €100-300, clinic visit €50-150. Private clinics in Rome/Milan €100-200 for consultation.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (farmacie) marked with green cross, widely available. Pharmacists are trained and can recommend OTC treatments. Night pharmacies rotate on a schedule posted on every pharmacy door.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Public hospitals provide good emergency care but can be crowded and slow. Private clinics (cliniche private) in major cities offer faster, English-speaking service. Northern Italy generally has better public healthcare than the south.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC. Non-EU visitors will be billed for non-emergency care.

controlledSubstances.note: Available OTC in low doses combined with paracetamol. Higher doses require prescription.
Prescription required. Carry original prescription and doctor's letter.

medications.generalAdvice: Most common medications available at pharmacies. Bring original packaging and prescriptions for controlled substances. Italian pharmacists are very knowledgeable and can often help with minor ailments.

scams.name: Friendship bracelet scam
scams.description: Men approach you and tie a 'friendship bracelet' on your wrist, then demand €10-20 payment. They target couples and solo women near tourist sites.
scams.avoidance: Keep hands in pockets near major monuments. Firmly say 'No' and walk away. Don't let anyone touch your wrist.

scams.name: Restaurant tourist trap
scams.description: Restaurants near major attractions charge €15-20 for a coffee or €50+ for a simple pasta. Menus may not show prices, or a 'coperto' (cover charge) and service charge are added.
scams.avoidance: Always check the menu and prices before sitting down. Eat where locals eat — one block off the main tourist street. 'Coperto' of €1-3 is normal; more than €5 is a tourist trap.

scams.name: Fake designer goods sellers
scams.description: Street vendors sell counterfeit bags, sunglasses, etc. While buying seems harmless, Italian law fines BUYERS of counterfeit goods up to €10,000.
scams.avoidance: Don't buy from street vendors. The fine applies to the buyer, not just the seller.

scams.name: Pickpocketing on public transit
scams.description: Professional pickpocket teams work crowded buses and metro lines, especially around Termini station in Rome. They use distraction techniques — bumping, spilling, asking questions.
scams.avoidance: Use a money belt or front pocket. Keep bags zipped and in front of you on transit. Be extra vigilant on Rome Metro Line A and the 64 bus to Vatican.

connectivity.simOptions: TIM, Vodafone, or WindTre SIM cards at airport shops or tabacchi. €10-20 for 30 days with 20-50GB. eSIM via Airalo or Holafly €5-12.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most hotels and restaurants. Public WiFi in some piazzas. Quality varies — can be slow.
connectivity.bestOption: TIM tourist SIM (best coverage) or eSIM. Buy at the airport — tabacchi shops may require an Italian tax code.

cultural.tipping: Not expected but appreciated. Round up the bill or leave €1-2 at restaurants. Coperto (cover charge) replaces the tip. No tipping at bars for coffee.
cultural.dressCode: Cover shoulders and knees at churches (strictly enforced at Vatican, Duomo). Smart casual for dinner — Italians dress well. Beach attire only at the beach.
cultural.greetings: Handshake for strangers. Friends do two cheek kisses (left then right). 'Buongiorno' until lunch, 'buonasera' after.
taboos: Ordering cappuccino after 11am (it's a breakfast drink)
Eating pizza with a knife and fork in Naples (use hands)
Rushing meals — lunch and dinner are social events
cultural.haggling: Not practiced. Prices are fixed in shops and restaurants. Only at outdoor flea markets.

safety.lgbtSafety: Legal but no same-sex marriage (civil unions since 2016). Major cities are tolerant — Rome, Milan, Bologna have active LGBTQ+ scenes. Rural south can be conservative.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe. May experience catcalling, especially in southern Italy. Avoid poorly lit areas at night. Tourist areas are well-policed.
safety.notes: Italy is very safe for tourists. Main risk is petty theft — especially pickpocketing in Rome, Naples, and Florence. Violent crime against tourists is rare.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free in Schengen area. UK: 90 days. EU: unlimited.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-June and September-October. July-August is hot, crowded, and many locals take vacation (some restaurants close).
